first.title: How slice::first works
first.description: The first item, as an Option (None for an empty slice).

note.text: safe: no panic on an empty slice

slides.caption: first() looks at index 0 if there is one.
The slice is not empty, so index 0 exists: 7.
For [] it would return None, where v[0] would panic.
The result is a reference, &7, printed as 7. last() works the same way from the other end.

last.title: How slice::last works
last.description: The last item, as an Option (None for an empty slice).

slides.caption: last() looks at index len() - 1, if the slice is not empty.
The length is 3, so the last index is 2: 9.
An empty slice gives None.
Unlike Iterator::last, slice::last is instant: it goes straight to the end.

get.title: How slice::get works
get.description: Reads an index safely: Some(item), or None when it is out of range.

slides.caption: get is the safe version of v[i]: instead of panicking, it returns None.
Index 1 exists: Some(20).
There is no index 5 (the last index is 2): None, no panic.
Use v[i] when the index must be valid (a bug otherwise), and get(i) when it may not be.

contains.title: How slice::contains works
contains.description: Checks whether an equal item is in the slice.

slides.caption: contains compares each item with 7, from the front.
3 is not 7.
7 equals 7: true, and the search stops.
contains looks at items one by one. For many lookups in a big collection, a HashSet is much faster.

windows.title: How slice::windows works
windows.description: Every run of n neighbouring items; the windows overlap.

note.text: a window of 2 sliding one step

slides.caption: windows(2) looks at 2 items at a time and slides one step to the right each time.
The first window: [1, 2].
It slides one step: [2, 3]. The 2 is used again.
[3, 4], and the window has reached the end.
A slice of length n gives n - size + 1 windows. Great for comparing neighbours: w[1] - w[0].

chunks.title: How slice::chunks works
chunks.description: Splits the slice into pieces of n items; the last piece may be shorter.

slides.caption: chunks(2) cuts the slice into consecutive pieces of 2.
[3, 4]. Unlike windows, no item is used twice.
Only 5 is left: the last chunk is just [5].
Use chunks_exact if every piece must have exactly n items; the leftovers are then available separately.

chunks_exact.title: How slice::chunks_exact works
chunks_exact.description: Pieces of exactly n items; leftovers are kept apart.

slides.caption: chunks_exact(2) yields only pieces of exactly 2 items.
5 cannot make a full piece: it is not yielded, but .remainder() returns it.
Because every chunk has the same length, the compiler can often make loops over chunks_exact faster.

split_at.title: How slice::split_at works
split_at.description: Divides a slice into two at an index; nothing is copied.

slides.caption: split_at(1) returns two views of the same memory: before index 1, and from index 1 on.
The left part ends just before index 1: [1].
The right part starts at index 1: [2, 3, 4].
Both parts borrow the original slice. An index past the end panics; split_at_checked returns an Option instead.

split_first.title: How slice::split_first works
split_first.description: The first item and the rest, or None if the slice is empty.

slides.caption: split_first separates the first item from the others.
The first item: 1.
The rest: [2, 3].
Handy in recursive code: if let Some((first, rest)) = s.split_first() { ... }.

binary_search.title: How slice::binary_search works
binary_search.description: Finds an item in a sorted slice by halving the search range each step.

slides.caption: binary_search never looks at every item. It checks the middle and throws away the half that cannot contain 9.
The middle is 7. 9 > 7, so 9 can only be in the right half.
The middle of what is left is 9: found at index 4.
If the item is missing, the result is Err(index where it would go): searching 4 gives Err(2). On an unsorted slice the result is meaningless.

binary_search_by_key.title: How slice::binary_search_by_key works
binary_search_by_key.description: Binary search on a key of each item; the slice must be sorted by that key.

slides.caption: binary_search_by_key compares the key (here the age, p.1) instead of the whole item.
The middle person, bo, is 30: that is the age searched for.
Found at index 1.
The slice must be sorted by the same key, for example with sort_by_key(|p| p.1).

partition_point.title: How slice::partition_point works
partition_point.description: The index of the first item for which the test becomes false.

slides.caption: All items that pass the test must come first. partition_point finds the border with a binary search.
1, 2 and 3 are < 5: they are before the border.
7 is the first item that is not < 5, at index 3.
partition_point is the insertion index: v.insert(3, 5) keeps the slice sorted.

sort_unstable.title: How slice::sort_unstable works
sort_unstable.description: Sorts in place, fast; equal items may change order.

slides.caption: sort_unstable rearranges the items inside the slice from smallest to largest.
1 is the smallest: it goes first.
Then 2.
And 3 last.
"Unstable" only means equal items may swap places. For plain numbers that is invisible, and it is faster than sort().

sort_unstable_by_key.title: How slice::sort_unstable_by_key works
sort_unstable_by_key.description: Sorts by a computed key, in place.

slides.caption: The closure gives each item a key (its length); the items are ordered by those keys.
"fig" has the smallest key, 3.
"pear": 4.
"banana": 6.
Use sort_by_key instead if words with the same length must keep their original order.

reverse.title: How slice::reverse works
reverse.description: Reverses the order of the items in place.

slides.caption: reverse swaps the first and last item, then the second and second-to-last, until it meets in the middle.
1 and 4 trade places.
2 and 3 trade places. The middle is reached.
reverse changes the slice itself. To read backwards without changing anything, use iter().rev().

rotate_left.title: How slice::rotate_left works
rotate_left.description: Shifts every item n places left; the ones that fall off the front go to the back.

slides.caption: rotate_left(2) moves everything 2 places to the left. The first 2 items wrap around to the end.
3, 4 and 5 move 2 places left.
1 and 2 fell off the front, so they go to the back.
rotate_right(2) does the opposite: [4, 5, 1, 2, 3]. No items are lost or copied.

swap.title: How slice::swap works
swap.description: Exchanges the items at two indexes.

slides.caption: swap(0, 2) trades the items at index 0 and index 2.
"a" and "c" change places.
"b" does not move.
You cannot write std::mem::swap(&mut v[0], &mut v[2]) (two mutable borrows of v), which is why slices have their own swap.

starts_with.title: How slice::starts_with works
starts_with.description: Checks whether the slice begins with the given items.

slides.caption: starts_with compares the first items of the slice with the prefix, in order.
2 == 2. The whole prefix matched: true.
ends_with checks the back the same way. An empty prefix always matches.

fill.title: How slice::fill works
fill.description: Overwrites every item with the same value.

slides.caption: fill(0) writes 0 into every place of the slice.
Every item is replaced by 0.
The length stays 3.
Works on part of a slice too: v[1..].fill(0) gives [1, 0, 0].

iter.title: How slice::iter works
iter.description: An iterator over references to the items; the slice stays usable.

title.text: for x in v.iter() { ... }   // v = vec![1, 2, 3]

slides.caption: iter() lends out each item as a reference, &i32. The Vec keeps ownership.
x is &1: a reference to the first item.
After the loop, v can still be used: nothing was moved out.
for x in &v is the same as for x in v.iter(). Use iter_mut() to change items, into_iter() to take them.

ends_with.title: How slice::ends_with works
ends_with.description: Checks whether the slice ends with the given items.

slides.caption: ends_with lines the suffix up with the end of the slice.
2 == 2 and 3 == 3: the end matches.
The 1 at the front does not matter.
An empty suffix always matches.

rotate_right.title: How slice::rotate_right works
rotate_right.description: Shifts every item n places right; the ones at the end wrap around to the front.

note.text: the last item comes to the front

slides.caption: rotate_right(1) moves every item one place right.
1, 2 and 3 move one place right.
4 falls off the end and wraps around to the front.
rotate_left(1) undoes it.

split.title: How slice::split works
split.description: Cuts a slice at every item that matches; the matches are dropped.

slides.caption: split works like str::split, but for any slice.
Before the first 0: [1].
Between the zeros: [2, 3].
After the last 0: [4]. The zeros themselves are not in any piece.
Each piece borrows the original slice: nothing is copied.

iter_mut.title: How slice::iter_mut works
iter_mut.description: An iterator of mutable references, to change items in place.

slides.caption: iter_mut lends out each item as &mut, so the loop can change it.
x points at 1; *x *= 10 makes it 10.
2 becomes 20, 3 becomes 30.
for x in &mut v is the same thing. The * is needed because x is a reference.

split_last.title: How slice::split_last works
split_last.description: The last item and everything before it.

slides.caption: split_last separates the final item from the others.
The last item: 3.
The rest: [1, 2].
None for an empty slice.

rchunks.title: How slice::rchunks works
rchunks.description: Like chunks, but starting from the end.

note.text: the short piece is at the front

slides.caption: rchunks cuts pieces of 2 from the back.
The last two: [4, 5].
Then [2, 3].
Only 1 is left: [1].
Useful for grouping digits from the right, like thousands separators.
